name: The Devils Club
overview: The Devils Club is a serious, remote Grade V alpine rock route up the roughly 2,000-2,500 ft east face of Southeast Mox Peak ("Hard Mox"), one of the most committing big walls in the Lower 48 given its approach. First climbed by Mike Layton and Eric (Erik) Wolfe over August 31-September 1, 2005, with one bivouac partway up the wall. Notably, the FA party topped out the East Face but — out of food and water — did not continue on to Southeast Mox's true summit; parties repeating the route should clarify whether their objective is the wall itself or the actual summit (which would require additional scrambling/climbing beyond the top of the face). A second-ascent party (Eric Wehrly, 2008) climbed a variation.
beta: Fred Beckey reportedly attempted this face earlier and found it traumatic enough to never return, and it came to be regarded as a last great problem perhaps best left unclimbed. Layton and Wolfe finally forced a route in 2005 after a brutal approach, climbing banded gneiss that offered very little solid protection; every hold reportedly required testing, and pitons often wouldn't set. Note: the grade/length is variously given as V+ 5.9+ A2- and ~2,500 ft, and as V+ 5.11- and 2,400 ft — the latter figures are used here, but treat the discrepancy as a sign of how approximate any grade is on this kind of loose, unrepeated wall.
descent_text: The East Face is rappelled top to bottom on its own line — there is no walk-off, and no fixed/bolted rappel stations exist anywhere on the route; every anchor is natural (slung horns, chockstones/gear anchors) built on the spot, so a party needs full natural-anchor-building skill and a rack sufficient to leave gear behind. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) rappelled the entire 2,400-2,500 ft face using two ropes tied together to maximize each rappel's reach, angling the line closer to the northeast ridge than their ascent line, especially on the lower half, to find sounder anchor rock and avoid the loosest terrain in the direct fall line. Their first rappel hung up and forced a strenuous full return to the top to free it before they could continue; from there, roughly a dozen more rappels (about 13 total) got them to the ground, finishing around 3:30 a.m. after an 18-hour continuous push from the base. At the bottom they waded back across the creek chest-deep rather than re-entering the alder/devil's club to reach their tent. Later parties should plan on a similar count (very roughly a dozen-plus rappels with a doubled/joined-rope setup) but treat that as an estimate scaled from a single documented descent, not a fixed number — anchor placement is judgment-call and can shift the rappel line and count. Expect loose, sometimes rotten rock the entire way (a defining hazard of the route), real risk of stuck ropes given the wandering natural-anchor line, and likely a night finish if the climb runs long, so headlamps and a plan for rope work in the dark should be assumed.
descent: Rappel the route from the top of the East Face using natural gear anchors (no bolts placed by the FA team); a full-length rope and a set of natural-anchor building skills (slung horns, gear anchors) are required since there are no fixed rap stations.
rappels: Rappel the East Face on its own line, about a dozen or more rappels on doubled ropes over roughly 2,400 ft, every anchor built from slung horns, chockstones and gear: there are no bolts anywhere on the route. No station list is published.
rappel_count_note: The only documented descent is the first ascent’s, which rappelled the face top to bottom on natural anchors, roughly a dozen-plus rappels; no station list or count has been published since, so none is shown. On that descent the first rappel hung up and had to be freed by climbing back to the top, and the anchors were angled toward the northeast ridge to find sounder rock than the ascent line.

pitch_detail.notes: Leaving the moat/talus at the toe of the East Face, the route starts up broken, blocky slab low on the wall; gear is spaced over lichen-covered rock as the line establishes itself above the approach.
Continued low-angle slab climbing on compact but featured rock; short discontinuous crack systems are linked with smeared friction moves.
An easier ramp/traverse picks the path of least resistance across a brushy, broken slab shelf, part of the extensive route-finding the FA party described on the lower wall.
The slab steepens; thin, discontinuous cracks are taken with small cams and nuts, with natural protection sparse and spaced.
A long run-out friction-slab pitch, the kind of ground the FA account describes covering efficiently (with simul-climbing) low on the 1,000-ft slab section beneath the headwall.
A short, steeper bulge breaks up the slab; positive edges allow pulling over onto easier ground above.
Moderate slab climbing resumes, weaving around loose blocks and lichen-covered patches typical of this remote, rarely-traveled face.
A steeper corner/crack splits the slab here; stemming and jamming past a small bulge is the crux move of the lower wall.
Slab climbing eases as the angle transitions toward the base of the headwall proper; broken ledges and ramps link the pitch together.
A short final pitch gains the small stance/bivy ledge at roughly 1,000 ft up the face, at the base of the 1,500-ft headwall, where the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) spent their one night out.
Leaving the bivy ledge, the headwall begins in earnest on a steep crack system; the rock here is noticeably more compact than the slabs below, though protection stays sparse.
Sustained crack and face climbing up the lower headwall, small cams and stoppers in a discontinuous crack; the wall's angle is now consistently steep.
A short, steep section past a bulge/mini-roof on face holds; gear thins out noticeably above the lip.

A corner system provides the natural line here; stemming and liebacking with protection that is adequate but spaced, consistent with the loose, poorly-protected character the FA team described of the wall overall.
Technical face climbing links small edges past a blank-looking section; noticeably harder than anything below and a preview of the difficulty concentrating higher on the headwall.
Continued corner and crack climbing higher on the headwall, with exposure mounting as the face steepens further toward vertical.
A strenuous crack pitch, hands to fists through a discontinuous system, with gear sparse but adequate for a committed leader.
Face climbing on knobs and edges links two crack systems; rock quality remains loose in places, and the headwall is steep, loose and poorly protected.
A steep face pitch on small wires and cams placed in shallow seams; the climbing is technical and increasingly run-out between placements.
The headwall steepens toward vertical as the party enters the upper third of the route; thin, technical climbing on marginal protection.

A traversing pitch searching out the line of weakness in an increasingly blank upper headwall, reflecting the real route-finding uncertainty the FA party described forcing their way through near the top.
A short, steep pitch gains a cramped stance below the final overhangs; belays through here are hanging or semi-hanging, built entirely from natural gear.
Sustained, strenuous climbing directly below the crux; rock quality improves slightly here but protection is still sparse ahead of the route's hardest moves.

The documented crux: the FA account describes surmounting the 'final overhangs' on this pitch with the leader unable to see where the next piece of protection would be. First climbed with a short aid section (recorded as 5.9+ A2-), later free ascents rate it around 5.11-; treat the X rating as literal on a route this remote.

An easy final pitch over loose, sandy stacked blocks tops out the East Face. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) stopped here rather than continuing to Hard Mox's true summit, out of food and water, marking their high point with a playing card before beginning the rappel descent.

fa: Mike Layton and Erik Wolfe, August 31-September 1, 2005
